title: 'Capturing Bigfoot' screening a homecoming for a Yakima story

content:
A reunion of sorts took place at the movie theater in Union Gap on Saturday. Not the kind for family or classmates, but for those who know the Yakima cowboys who made one of the most famous video clips of all time.  

The minute-long Patterson-Gimlim footage, named for Yakima residents Roger Patterson and Bob Gimlin, purportedly showed a female Bigfoot walking along a creek bed in northern California on Oct. 20, 1967.  

That short film made money — the footage was worked into a movie that screened across the country and raked in the modern day equivalent of millions of dollars — but it also strained the relationships of those who were associated with it for decades.

A special screening of “Capturing Bigfoot,” a new documentary about Roger Patterson and his friends, took place at The Majestic movie theater on Saturday. The documentary explores the film’s impact on the lives of those involved in it and their families, and features newly found footage of what appears to be a rehearsal of the original film.

“It’s like a homecoming for the film," said director Marq Evans, who has been traveling for screenings the past several weeks from Los Angeles to Montana. 

The documentary has received national media attention and was released for streaming on Amazon Prime Video on Oct. 20.

Other people who worked on or were featured in the documentary attended the Union Gap screening: producer Tamir Ardon; Clint Patterson, son of Roger Patterson and a main focus of the documentary; Vaile Thompson, nephew of Roger Patterson and Al DeAtley; and Bob Heironimus.

The original 1967 footage was made by Roger Patterson and Gimlin. It featured Heironimus wearing the bigfoot costume. DeAtley, a prominent Yakima businessman and brother-in-law to Roger Patterson, helped finance it. 

Clint Patterson, of Wilsall, Mont., told the Yakima Herald-Republic that it took months for the filmmakers to earn his trust to tell his story.

Roger died in 1972 when Clint was young, and he never told him that the film was a hoax. Finally, his mother, Patricia, admitted to him that it was Heironimus in the suit. He said he was devastated that his father never let him in on the secret before his passing.

Clint had been wanting to tell the world that it was a hoax, as many people continue to defend the film’s authenticity. His mother wrote him a letter to say she would disown him if he went public with the truth.

The documentary captures the moments where Clint reunites with and makes amends with his mother and Heironimus.

"It's brought a lot of people together, a lot that haven't seen each other in years," Clint said. "I'm really glad that I've been able to come out and tell the truth and get this monkey off my back."

Gimlin, however, never quite admitted to the filmmakers that it was a hoax.

Heironimus and Gimlin are neighbors in town, and still have not repaired their old friendship, Heironimus said.

Glenda Heironimus, Bob's wife, said that most of the people in the audience that night had known about Bob's role for decades. 

"The whole Ahtanum Valley has known for years," she said. 

The "Capturing Bigfoot" screening coincided with the Greater Yakima Chamber of Commerce's Yakima Valley Bigfoot Con over the weekend, but was unaffiliated. 

After the movie screening, attendees gathered at the Old Town Pump Saloon in Union Gap.

What does Bigfoot like to drink? Heironimus prefers a whisky soda with a splash of Pepsi, he said. 

Questen Inghram is a reporter at the Yakima Herald-Republic whose beat focuses on water, the environment, and Lower Valley communities. Email qinghram@yakimaherald.com or call 509-577-7674.
